messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Threat
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Threat
  - Negative Appraisals → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Negative Appraisals → Threat
  - Negative Appraisals → Triggers
  - Threat → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Negative Appraisals

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Maui’s daughter, Leilani, was seven when the leukemia appeared, a word he had never spoken aloud before the pediatric oncologist said it in a room that smelled of antiseptic and fear. He remembers the exact shape of the doctor’s mouth forming the syllables, and how his own chest went tight, as though the air had been siphoned from the room. For eighteen months, he sat beside her bed in the pediatric intensive care unit, watching monitors beep and drip, learning the precise pitch of a code blue alarm. He held her hand during lumbar punctures, counting her breaths when the sedation made her stop breathing for seconds that felt like hours. She survived. He did not. What survived was a man who now, eight years later, cannot walk past a hospital without his throat closing, who finds himself gripping the steering wheel so hard his knuckles blanch whenever a delivery truck idles too long at a light.

Maui had been a project manager for thirty years, a man who built timelines and met deadlines, who believed that if you planned carefully enough, nothing truly bad could happen. The illness had shattered that belief. Now, when a colleague’s email goes unanswered for an hour, his stomach drops and he is certain—certain—that something catastrophic has occurred. He has come to see delay as a signal of disaster, a direct line from a late reply to a child’s flatlined heart monitor. The physical reactions arrive without warning: a tightness in his ribs when he hears a siren, a cold sweat when he catches the scent of hand sanitizer. He knows, intellectually, that these are memories, but in his body they are present tense. He has learned to keep his mind occupied constantly—podcasts during his commute, music while he cooks, the television on all night so he does not lie in the dark replaying the moment the doctor said *we need to talk*—because when his thoughts go quiet, the images return. He tries hard not to think about the trauma. He has been trying for eight years.

The self-blame is the part he cannot outrun. He was the one who noticed the bruises and dismissed them as playground scrapes, who told himself she was just tired, who waited three extra days before calling the pediatrician. He had failed to protect her. He had acted wrongly, and the consequence had been her suffering. This conviction has reshaped how he moves through the world: he no longer trusts his own judgment. When his adult son mentions a headache, Maui spends the rest of the day in a state of quiet dread, certain he will miss the warning signs again. He has come to believe that he cannot trust himself to do the right thing. This belief drives him to avoid all medical environments entirely—he has not had a physical exam in six years, he crosses the street to avoid walking past the hospital where Leilani was treated, and when his primary care office called to schedule a routine colonoscopy, he did not return the call. He tells himself it is easier not to know. What he means is that he is afraid of what he might fail to notice next.

The cycle tightens in the ordinary moments. A few months ago, his car made a rattling sound on the highway. He pulled over, heart pounding, certain the engine was about to fail, convinced he would be stranded, that something terrible was unfolding because he had not prevented it. The car was fine. But the feeling did not leave. He had already begun scanning the dashboard for the next warning light, already rehearsing the catastrophe. That evening, sitting alone in his quiet house, he thought about the oncologist’s face again, and he felt the familiar wave of shame: he should have known sooner, should have acted faster, should have been a different kind of father. The thought led him to turn on the television and scroll through his phone simultaneously, filling every channel of attention so the memory could not land. He did not sleep well that night. He rarely does.

What finally brought him to seek help was not his own distress but a phone call from his daughter. She is pregnant now, due in four months. She asked him to be in the delivery room. He said yes immediately, then spent the next week unable to eat, his chest constricted by a fear he could not name aloud. He is terrified that he will freeze, that he will see the medical equipment and the monitors and the controlled urgency of the staff and be transported back to that room, that he will fail her again. He is hoping that a therapist can teach him how to stay present. He is afraid that nothing will.
